# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits under the title, and the deciding count '4 beliefs: 4 holding' is beside it, tied by the line that the verdict is the worst of its cards.
screens.why_b2: Each card gives what was counted, out of how many and the bar, but the Importance card prints '6 of 6 put it in their two' twice and the Frequency line packs median, inside-count, bar and 'at the bar' into one string I had to read twice.
screens.why_b3: Importance and Current solution are my checked lines word for word, Prevalence and Frequency are my 8-in-10 and 4-to-7-days beliefs, and the statement uses my own table, theatre and '20% at best' words.
screens.why_b4: The page says nothing about what four holding beliefs mean for AirCaps or what I should do next, such as moving on to the solution stage or watching the Frequency belief that only just held.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 is visible and Frequency is honestly marked 'at the bar', but the page never says seven people is a small sample, and a belief that only just held gets the same 'Holding up' as 7 of 7.
screens.instead: Holding up on 7 people, a small sample: all four beliefs held, but Frequency only reached the bar (4 of 6), so the problem looks real enough to test the glasses next, and Frequency should be rechecked with more people.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside '7 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7', so I see both the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The strip runs 0 to 7 with seven for-cells and my bar marked at 6 of 7 (at least 8 in 10), so what is counted, over how many people and where the bar sits are plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: Prevalence and 'at least 8 in 10' are mine, but the belief line drops my segment's qualifiers ('in the US who talk with hearing people every week'), and the stray '— the most recent time it happened' after the yes/no gate reads oddly.
screens.why_b4: 'Common among these 7' plus a pointer to the next two cards tells me where to look, not what this means for AirCaps, for example that the wedge is real but every person said yes.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and the claim is kept to 'these 7', so nothing overreaches.
screens.instead: At least 8 in 10 of deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week lost track of a conversation in the last 7 days: Holding up, 7 of 7 said yes against a bar of 6. Only 7 answered, so it's a lean: the problem is common in my wedge, and frequency and importance on the next cards decide whether it's worth building for.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 4 of 6 against a bar of 4 of 6, marked at the bar, so I know it held and by exactly how much.
screens.why_b2: The strip makes the count and bar plain, but the axis starts at 0 though nobody could answer 0, and the legend's 'at what you said' versus 'what you said' takes a second look.
screens.why_b3: Frequency and my 4 to 7 days out of 7 are mine, and 'lose track of a conversation with hearing people' is the event I checked.
screens.why_b4: 'Whether it matters is the next card' points onward but does not say what holding exactly at the bar means for my wedge.
screens.why_b5: The small group is called a lean, but 'the most recent time it happened' under a seven-day count question misdescribes what was asked, and one answer moving would flip the result.
screens.instead: Holding, just: 4 of 6 lose track on 4 or more days a week, the bar exactly, so one person fewer and it would not hold; Harriet and Ruth, at theatres and seminars, hit it less often, so test whether the weekly rhythm is the table and not the big room.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 6 put it in their two and bar 4 of 6, so I know it held and by how much, though the 6 of 6 line is printed twice.
screens.why_b2: The caption says 6 people, two picks each, 12 picks counted, my row is marked as the problem I named with 6, and the strip shows 6 for against a marker at 4.
screens.why_b3: Importance and the belief line, five things hard when a conversation with hearing people is too fast or too noisy, with following a fast, noisy conversation in their two, are word for word what I checked.
screens.why_b4: The So line rightly says top two, not first, but it never says what that means for AirCaps, such as leading with group conversation and watching getting a word in, picked by 3 of 6, as the next pain.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, Eleanor's guess is excluded and named, the small group is called a lean, not a call, and the So line refuses to claim it ranks first.
screens.instead: All 6 put following a fast, noisy conversation in their two, a lean from a small group; lead with it, and note that getting a word in at the right moment came next for 3 of 6, worth a feature or a follow-up question.

screens.why_b1: 'Holding up' sits right beside '5 of 6 said today's way falls short · bar 4 of 6', so I know it held and by how much it cleared the bar.
screens.why_b2: The five rungs show their counts and for/against marks, my line is drawn under 'Missed a little, caught up quickly', and the strip shows 5 for, 1 against with the marker at 4 of 6, all readable on first look.
screens.why_b3: The card is named Current solution and the belief line is word for word the one I checked about following hearing people around a noisy table.
screens.why_b4: The So line names the gap (3 caught the gist but missed details, 2 nodded along, none lost it entirely), but 'your solution is judged against this gap on the next study' doesn't tell me the bar my glasses must clear, which is the details people miss.
screens.why_b5: 7 answered and 6 counted are both visible, Eleanor's guess is set apart, and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' keeps a 5-of-6 result from being sold as strong.
screens.instead: Say the next step concretely: most already catch the gist and lose the details, so the glasses must win on the details (names, numbers, side remarks), not on rescuing people who follow nothing; also ask about the last group conversation, not just 'your last conversation'.

screens.why_b1: The box opens on 'Holding up' with '5 of 6 said today's way falls short · bar 4 of 6' right beside it, and the heading 'Current solution held, 5 of 6' ties the number to the verdict.
screens.why_b3: 'Current solution' and the belief line about following hearing people around a noisy table are word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what the one dissent means for AirCaps, such as whether people deaf on one side are a weaker fit for the wedge, so I am left to work out the next step myself.
screens.why_b5: The count line shows 1 against out of 6 and the group is labelled (1), so nothing claims more than one person said; the stray 'Missed a little, caught up quickly / against' tag under the quote is confusing but does not overstate anything.
screens.why_b6: Tomás's end-seat trick, keeping everyone on his good side, is a workaround I never typed, and it hints that people with hearing loss in one ear manage well enough without us.
screens.instead: Say that the one person whose way works is deaf on one side and manages by where he sits, so weigh tightening the segment toward hearing loss in both ears; and note that Importance has no box because nobody said no there.

screens.why1: As the first screen, it plainly checks that I am someone who talks with hearing people, which is what this study is about.
screens.why2: 'Hearing people' is the word we use ourselves, and the question is short and clear on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know without guessing whether I talk with hearing people in a week: at work, in shops, with family.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it completely for a gate, and a gate takes no escape.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment wording ('talk with hearing people every week') and leaks nothing of a product or a plan.
screens.why6: One short question with two options is easy to hold by ear, though plain 'Yes or no' would sound more natural than 'I'll read 2 options'.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you talk face to face with any hearing people? Yes / No

screens.why1: Right after I said I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to ask whether one of those conversations got away from me this past week.
screens.why2: "Lose track of a conversation" is exactly how I'd put it when people talk too fast or over noise and I miss where it went.
screens.why3: I know straight away whether I lost the thread at dinner, at work or at the counter this week, because it's my own life.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it: some weeks I follow everything with lipreading or captions and some weeks I don't, and the story chips belong to the box after a Yes, not to this question.
screens.why5: It asks about the problem itself, not following a fast or noisy conversation, and nothing about a product, captions or the company's plans comes through to me.
screens.why6: "In the last 7 days, did you lose track of a conversation with hearing people? Yes or no." is short, one question and easy to answer from one hearing (or one look at the screen).
screens.why7: The gate asks the costly thing, losing track, inside the 7-day window, not the circumstance everyone in the segment shares, so a deaf person who followed everything can truly say No and the rest of us Yes, with two fixed answers and no escape.

screens.why1: Right after I said yes, I lost track of a conversation this week, so asking how many days that happened is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: Losing track of a conversation with hearing people is exactly how I'd put it, and counting days in the last week is easy to grasp on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know which days I sat at work or at the shop and lost the thread, so I can count them from my own week.
screens.why4: One button per day from 1 to 7, with no zero since I already said yes, covers every true answer without overlap, and I can't recall sits apart.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's event, losing track of a conversation with hearing people, and nothing of a product or plan reaches me.
screens.why6: One short question, then 'say a number from 1 to 7, or say you can't recall', is easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: Every option counts days on the window's unit, from 1 up to the window's 7, the unit is said once, the event is a single act on a given day, and the only escape is I can't recall, as the card requires.

screens.why1: Right after I've said how often I lost track, it makes sense to ask which part of these conversations I'd most like made easier.
screens.why2: I can follow it on one read, and these are the words I'd use myself: following, getting a word in, worn out.
screens.why3: I know which of these wears on me, so I can answer from my own week.
screens.why4: Two options aren't part of my last conversation with hearing people: phone and video calls, and announcements in shops and stations. 'Not being worn out' also reads backwards after 'made easier'.
screens.why5: The study is about talking face to face, but the phone, video and announcement rows drift into other channels and settings the founder didn't mean.
screens.why6: One short question and five short options I can hold, with the escape said last.
screens.why7: The own row, following a fast, noisy conversation, is there and not first, and 'None of these' is offered. But two rivals belong to another channel or setting, the card's named pitfall, which leaves only two true rivals in face-to-face talk.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Following a fast, noisy conversation · Getting a word in at the right moment · Keeping up when people talk over each other · Catching what someone says from across the room · Staying with it without getting worn out · None of these

screens.why1: After asking how often I lost track and what I'd most like made easier, it makes sense to ask how my last conversation actually went.
screens.why2: 'How did following what hearing people said around a noisy table go' piles up and needs a second read, and 'your last conversation' then turning into 'a noisy table' makes me stop and work out which one they mean.
screens.why3: My last conversation with hearing people was at the pharmacy counter, not a noisy table, so I'd have to guess whether to answer about that one or think back to the last dinner.
screens.why4: The five run cleanly from following nearly everything to not following at all, 'mostly nodded along' is exactly what I do, and 'I can't recall' fits since nobody can follow a conversation for me.
screens.why5: The founder's 'too fast or too noisy' has narrowed to 'a noisy table', which leaves out the fast one-to-one talk where I lose track just as often.
screens.why6: The options say well as a list I can hold, but the stem is a mouthful to hear once and the noisy table arrives late, after I've already pictured a different conversation.
screens.why7: It is one measure, how much I followed, with two working rungs above the line, a total failure last, and the right escape, but 'Lost the thread and mostly nodded along' joins two states with 'and', which the card forbids.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. How much of it did you follow? Followed nearly everything · Missed a little, caught up quickly · Caught the gist, missed the details · Lost the thread most of the way · Could not follow it at all · or I can't recall
